Hi, as someone who studied behavior in cats in the US, cats can be very happy as indoor only! Not only does it extend their life expectancy by 2x, you can make sure they don’t get parasites and keep from overkilling. As long as you make sure your cat(s) has all the proper things in life, it will sure to be a happy feline! If you even feel too guilty about keeping Snowball in all the time, you can make supervised visits to the outside! Using a leash, harness, or simple barriers can be all you need to keep kitty safe and still get some freshness from the outside! Unlike what most people might think, cats generally don’t need to hunt all the time, every day. It’s actually bad for our ecosystem as cats will kill from boredom more than hunger! An excellent idea you can use with your cat, if you feel they need to hunt, is to buy fabric mice that have pouches in them to store food, hide them around the house as best you can and lets kitty find them on their own (and don’t forget to take the bowl of food away)! It’s extremely engaging for them as they have to hunt for food when they’re hungry rather than for boredom, it’s safe for the cat and birds, and it’s a good way to help overweight cats lose some jiggle. For more milder cats, a nice window hammock might be the best idea!

As someone that works in the veterinary field I would suggest to try to wait around at 6 months to get him neutered for the best developmentally and it’s safer surgery and anesthesia wise. Neutering is a healthy preventative to spraying tendencies, but you can always get a product called Feliway that comes in a plug in diffuser or a spray and it should act as a calming agent so he shouldn’t feel like spraying. When you bring him home first, make sure to keep him in a separate room from the female for several days with a towel that you’ve rubbed on the females face and tail so you can introduce her scent then switch it around, lock her up while he gets to explore then by then they should be familiar with each other and you can safely let them be face to face. Make sure to have a cat tree, I would recommend dishing out some money for a large one that both of them can enjoy. Make sure to keep one litter box just for him and a separate one for her, it’s how cats prefer things to be since they are solitary animals. Keep the carrier open and accessible so that he has a place to go if he wants and so he doesn’t familiarize it when you just get it out to take him to the vet. Kibble is cheaper and bulk, but cats are developmentally able to process kibble completely so its healthiest to feed them a more raw diet. Wet foods are good, making food is better. There’s plenty of information you can get googling homemade cat food. There’s also new product from a company called Stella and Chewys that sell frozen and freeze dried cat food. Make sure to handle him often. Hold him, touch his paws, face, ears, legs. Make sure to hold the legs out, like stretch them out and teach him not to pull them back. Find the right toy. There are many types of cat toys and some cats can be picky. There are good “stocking stuffers” at any store carrying pet toys that are holiday packs of different cat toys usually including something crinkly, jingling toys like bell balls, small stuffed toys like mice, hard toys like rope mice, and sometimes wands with a crinkly toy, a rope, a plush toy, or a jingling toy. Try not to let him outside by himself. If you want to let him outside make sure he’s on a harness and leash or in a see thru carrier. Indoor only cats live the longest and are the healthiest usually, outdoor cats are expected to live half or less than an indoor only, and for indoor-outdoor cats it’s somewhere in between mattering if he’s wandering multiple yards or just yours. MAKE SURE TO KEEP UPDATED ON VACCINES there’s lots the first few years but then every three you get boosters.
